pamphlet_excerpts: Understanding Paint Sheen: Sheen is a critical characteristic that refers to the degree of shine or gloss of any coating or surface (p. 43).
Existing Sheen Impact: The sheen currently on the surface can determine the amount of surface preparation required (p. 43).
Durability and Appearance: The abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, and overall beauty of the painted area (p. 43).
Full Sheen Spectrum: The typical full sheen range, from lowest to highest, includes flat or matte, eggshell or low luster, satin or pearl, semi gloss, and high or full gloss (p. 43).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Evaluate Durability Needs: The abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, and overall beauty of the painted area (p. 43).
Step 2 - Compare Gloss Levels: The typical full sheen range, from lowest to highest, includes flat or matte, eggshell or low luster, satin or pearl, semi gloss, and high or full gloss (p. 43).
Step 3 - Check Manufacturer Standards: Because there are no industry wide standard definitions of these terms, gloss levels may vary from one manufacturer to another (p. 43).
Step 4 - Match Sheen to Surface: The type of sheen you choose will depend on what you are painting (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Primer as Final Prep: Applying primer, the first coat of paint, also is the last stage of surface preparation (p. 51).
Bonding and Sealing Functions: The primer makes the next coat stick to the surface, protects the substrate, and seals the surface (p. 51).
Substrate-Specific Primers: There are different primers for wood, concrete and masonry, plaster and drywall, steel, and other metals (p. 51).
Indoor and Outdoor Wood Primers: Wood primers are available in oil-based or water-based products and can be used indoors or outdoors (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Substrate Primer: There are different primers for wood, concrete and masonry, plaster and drywall, steel, and other metals (p. 51).
Step 2 - Prime Bare Wood Surfaces: Wood primers are available in oil-based or water-based products and can be used indoors or outdoors (p. 51).
Step 3 - Apply Alkali-Resistant Masonry Primer: Exterior masonry surfaces are often highly alkaline, so be sure to use primers on surfaces that are alkali-resistant (p. 51).
Step 4 - Remove Loose Plaster Dust: Make sure primers for plaster surfaces are alkali-resistant and that plaster dust is removed first (p. 51).
